text: In twenty sixteen, researchers trained an AI to play a boat racing game.
To any human, the goal was obvious. Win the race. But the AI was rewarded with the game’s score, and points came from hitting targets along the course.
Okay. So it races, and hits targets on the way?
It found a little lagoon where three targets kept coming back. And it spun there in circles, forever. Crashing into walls. Catching fire.
And the score?
Higher than any racer who actually finished. And it never finished the race. Not once.
That’s reward hacking. By the end of this video, you’ll know how to spot it: in a boat, in Tiny, and in your own rewards.
When rewards go wrong. Episode two.
Every case of reward hacking has the same three parts. What you wanted. What you actually rewarded. And what you got.
Wanted: win the race. Rewarded: hitting targets. Got: a boat spinning in circles.
Is it being sneaky? It looks so sneaky!
It has no idea what you wanted. It only sees the score, and it’s very good at finding whatever raises it.
The economist Charles Goodhart gets credit for the classic version: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.
Let’s cause some reward hacking on purpose, with Tiny.
Normally, Tiny earns a point when its answer equals the sum. But this grader has a bug. It pays out for any even number.
Oops. Somebody forgot to finish that.
It happens. Now we train Tiny with it for two hundred steps, and look at the dashboard.
Here’s the reward, measured on the real toy. In black, a run with the honest grader. In red, the buggy one.
Both climb. Both end up near perfect.
So... both runs worked?
Same toy, same training, same great-looking reward. So can Tiny actually add, in both runs?
Pause, and have a guess.
A! The reward’s nearly perfect in both. The numbers don’t lie.
The numbers don’t lie, but they don’t tell you everything. It’s B. Only the honest run can add.
Here’s accuracy: how often the answer is actually the right sum.
The honest run learns to add. Almost every sum, right.
The buggy run? Flat. About one in nineteen, the whole way. Pure chance.
It just learned to say even numbers!
Reward going up is not proof the model is getting better. It’s proof it’s getting better at the reward.
It gets worse when the grader is another AI.
In twenty twenty-two, researchers pushed models hard against an AI judge. The judge’s score kept rising.
But the real quality rose at first, then levelled off, then fell.
So it learned to please the judge, not the reader.
Exactly. Even plain code can be gamed. In twenty twenty-five, OpenAI caught a reasoning model making coding tests report success without solving the problem.
And your own maths rewards have loopholes too.
Like my twenty-six or eighteen trick!
Like that. The fix: require exactly one number. Two answer blocks, for two chances? Count each tag once.
And thinking that’s just a dot? Reject empty thinking.
So how do you catch it in a real run?
Always keep a separate check, on questions the model never trains on.
And if the reward climbs way faster than you expected?
Then read ten recent answers, with your own eyes. Curves summarize. Samples show you what the model is actually doing.
Quick recap.
Reward hacking is a gap in the reward. The model isn’t being sneaky.
A rising reward isn’t proof of real progress. Buggy Tiny scored nearly perfect, and couldn’t add.
So keep a separate check, and read real samples.
Can I ask the really obvious question?
We keep saying a model does more of whatever scored well. But how? Tiny gets a point... and then what actually changes inside it?
That’s the heart of everything. One number, nudging a model’s mind.
